# Introduction

Bash is both a command-line shell and a scripting language. Even if you mostly
use it to launch tools, a little scripting can make repetitive work safer and
more reproducible. This lesson builds on basic command-line familiarity and
covers common techniques for working with file names, collections, and batches
of commands.

# Formatting long commands

A backslash (`\`) at the very end of a line tells Bash that the command
continues on the next line. This can make long commands easier to read,
especially when they have several options or arguments. Put one logical
argument or option on each continued line and indent continuation lines
consistently.

The backslash must be the final character on the line: trailing spaces after
it can prevent the continuation from working as intended. Do not put a comment
after a continuation backslash, because the comment consumes the next line.

```{bash}
find fastq \
    -type f \
    -name '*.fastq.gz' \
    -print0 \
  | wc -l
```

For commands where options and arguments can be listed separately, this style
also makes it easier to add or remove an option without changing the rest of
the command.

```{bash}
tar -czvf \
    project-files.tar.gz \
    results/ \
    scripts/ \
    README.md
```

# Variables and text expansion

## Scalar variables

A scalar variable stores one value, such as a sample name or path. Assignments
*must not have spaces around `=`*. Use `$name` or, preferably in longer
expressions, `${name}` to expand a variable.

Single and double quotes have different meanings in Bash. **Double quotes**
preserve the value as one argument while still allowing variable and command
substitution. **Single quotes** preserve everything between them literally:
variables are not expanded. The quote marks themselves are syntax and are not
included in the resulting value. In most scripts, use double quotes around
variable expansions so spaces and wildcard characters in a value do not get
treated as argument separators or filename patterns.

```{bash}
sample="patient 01"
double_quoted="Sample: $sample"
single_quoted='Sample: $sample'
input_file="data/${sample}/reads_R1.fastq.gz"

printf 'Sample: %s\n' "$sample"
printf 'Double quotes: %s\n' "$double_quoted"
printf 'Single quotes: %s\n' "$single_quoted"
printf 'Input:  %s\n' "$input_file"
```

Prefer `printf` over `echo` in scripts when you need predictable handling of
backslashes or option-like text. The `printf` format string above is
single-quoted because its `%s` and `\n` should be interpreted by `printf`,
while the values passed to it are double-quoted so each remains a single
argument.

## Arrays

An indexed array holds an ordered list of values, unlike a scalar variable,
which holds one value. Arrays are useful when a script needs to process a
known set of samples or files. Declare array items separated by spaces; use
`"${array[@]}"` when passing all items so that each item remains a distinct
argument, even if it contains spaces.

```{bash}
project="rnaseq-study"                 # one scalar value
samples=("sample 01" "sample-02" "sample-03")

printf 'Project: %s\n' "$project"
printf 'Number of samples: %s\n' "${#samples[@]}"
printf 'First sample: %s\n' "${samples[0]}"
printf 'Samples: %s\n' "${samples[@]}"
```

Bash array indices start at zero. `${#samples[@]}` gives the number of array
items; `${samples[0]}` accesses the first. Avoid writing `${samples}` when you
mean the whole array: use `"${samples[@]}"` to preserve item boundaries.

## Command substitution

Command substitution runs a command and replaces `$(...)` with the command's
output. This lets a script save a result for later use. It is often used to
count files, capture a date, or save the output of a short query. Quote the
result when using it so spaces in the value remain intact.

```{bash}
sample_count=$(wc -l < bash/samples.tsv)
today=$(date +%F)

printf 'Lines in sample table: %s\n' "$sample_count"
printf 'Date: %s\n' "$today"
```

If a command prints several simple, whitespace-separated values, wrapping its
command substitution in parentheses assigns those words to an indexed array.
For example, this reads the sample IDs from the first column of the TSV:

```{bash}
sample_ids=( $(awk -F '\t' 'NR > 1 { print $1 }' bash/samples.tsv) )

printf 'Found %s samples\n' "${#sample_ids[@]}"
printf 'Sample: %s\n' "${sample_ids[@]}"
```

This form uses Bash word splitting and filename expansion on the command's
output. Use it only when you know the output contains simple values without
spaces or wildcard characters; it is not safe for arbitrary file paths. For
line-oriented output that may contain spaces, use `mapfile` to preserve each
line as one array item:

```{bash}
mapfile -t sample_ids < <(awk -F '\t' 'NR > 1 { print $1 }' bash/samples.tsv)
```

Command substitution removes trailing newline characters from the output.
Avoid using it to collect arbitrary file paths into one string: splitting that
string later can break names containing spaces or other special characters.
Use an array or a NUL-delimited loop for lists of files.

## Removing parts of a value with parameter expansion

Bash can remove matching text from the beginning or end of a variable without
starting another program. The pattern is a shell glob pattern, not a regular
expression. For a suffix, `%` removes the *shortest* matching ending and `%%`
removes the *longest* matching ending. For a prefix, `#` removes the shortest
match and `##` the longest.

For example, `${my_var%%.txt}` removes a `.txt` suffix if it is present. Since
that pattern is exactly `.txt`, it does not remove other text before the suffix.
Use a wildcard when the part to remove can vary.

```{bash}
my_var="long/path/to/results/sample.counts.txt.txt"

printf '%s\n' "${my_var%%.txt*}"    # long/path/to/results/sample.counts
printf '%s\n' "${my_var%.txt*}"     # long/path/to/results/sample.counts.txt
printf '%s\n' "${my_var%.*}"        # long/path/to/results/sample.counts.txt
printf '%s\n' "${my_var%%.*}"       # long/path/to/results/sample
printf '%s\n' "${my_var##*/}"       # sample.counts.txt.txt
printf '%s\n' "${my_var#*/}"        # path/to/results/sample.counts.txt.txt
```

This is handy for making output names from input names. Consider which suffix
you want to strip: a compressed FASTQ file may have a name ending in
`.fastq.gz`, so `${file%.gz}` and `${file%.*}` produce different results.

```{bash}
file="reads/sample_R1.fastq.gz"
uncompressed_name="${file%.gz}"
sample_name="${file##*/}"
sample_name="${sample_name%%_*}"

printf 'Uncompressed name: %s\n' "$uncompressed_name"
printf 'Sample name:       %s\n' "$sample_name"
```

Bash also supports pattern substitution with `${variable/pattern/replacement}`.
The pattern uses shell glob syntax, not a regular expression. A single `/`
replaces the first match; `//` replaces every match. This is useful for
changing text inside a value, while prefix/suffix removal is usually clearer
when changing a file extension.

```{bash}
my_var="results/sample.txt"
first_replacement="${my_var/txt/tsv}"

printf '%s\n' "$first_replacement"  # results/sample.tsv

text="txt and txt"
all_replacements="${text//txt/tsv}"
printf '%s\n' "$all_replacements"   # tsv and tsv

output_file="${my_var%.txt}.tsv"
printf '%s\n' "$output_file"        # results/sample.tsv
```

In `${my_var/txt/tsv}`, Bash searches for the first substring matching `txt`.
Because that pattern can match in the middle of a longer string, stripping a
known suffix and appending a new one (as in `output_file`) is often more
precise for file extensions.

# The `PATH` environment variable

`PATH` is a colon-separated list of directories that the shell searches when
you type a command name. If an executable is not in one of those directories,
the shell may report “command not found.” Use `command -v` to see which
executable would run, and `printf` to inspect the current search path.

```{bash}
printf '%s\n' "$PATH"
command -v bash
command -v python
```

If you install a program in a personal `bin` directory, prepend that directory
to `PATH` so it is searched before the other locations. This change applies to
the current shell and programs launched from it. Do not replace `PATH` with
only one directory, since that can make standard commands unavailable. On an
HPC cluster, use the site-recommended module or environment setup when
available.

```{bash}
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
command -v my_tool
```

# Loops

## `for` loops

Use a `for` loop to repeat an operation over array items, file names, or a
sequence of values. The example below prints intended work rather than running
a bioinformatics program. Quoting `"$sample"` is important if a value contains
spaces or shell-special characters.

```{bash}
samples=("sample_A" "sample_B" "sample_C")

for sample in "${samples[@]}"; do
    echo "Would align ${sample}_R1.fastq.gz and ${sample}_R2.fastq.gz"
done
```

For file lists, a glob such as `*.fastq.gz` is convenient when files are in one
directory. If no file matches, Bash normally leaves the glob unchanged; check
that files were found before using this pattern in a real script. Do not use
`for file in $(find ...)`: command substitution splits file names on whitespace.

```{bash}
shopt -s nullglob
files=(fastq/*.fastq.gz)

if ((${#files[@]} == 0)); then
    printf 'No FASTQ files found in fastq/\n' >&2
else
    for file in "${files[@]}"; do
        printf 'Found: %s\n' "$file"
    done
fi
```

## Conditional tests with `if`

Loops often need to make decisions about each item. In Bash, `[[ ... ]]`
performs a conditional test; `if` runs its body when the test succeeds. File
tests such as `-f` and `-d` are useful for checking expected inputs before
processing them. Quote variable expansions even inside `[[ ... ]]` as a clear
habit, especially when reusing the value in commands.

```{bash}
if [[ -f "bash/samples.tsv" ]]; then
    printf 'The sample table is a regular file\n'
fi

if [[ -d "bash" ]]; then
    printf 'The bash/ directory exists\n'
fi
```

Common tests and operators include:

| Test or operator               | Meaning                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-e PATH`                      | Path exists.                                                                                |
| `-f PATH`                      | Path exists and is a regular file.                                                          |
| `-d PATH`                      | Path exists and is a directory.                                                             |
| `-r PATH`                      | Path is readable by the current process.                                                    |
| `-w PATH`                      | Path is writable by the current process.                                                    |
| `-s PATH`                      | Path is a regular file with nonzero size.                                                   |
| `-z STRING`                    | String is empty.                                                                            |
| `-n STRING`                    | String is not empty.                                                                        |
| `STRING1 == STRING2`           | Strings are equal.                                                                          |
| `STRING1 != STRING2`           | Strings are different.                                                                      |
| `! TEST`                       | Negates a test.                                                                             |
| `TEST1 && TEST2`               | Both tests must succeed.                                                                    |
| `TEST1 || TEST2`               | At least one test must succeed.                                                             |
| `(( NUMBER1 >= NUMBER2 ))`     | Numeric comparison; arithmetic operators include `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=`.      |

Use `[[ ... ]]` for file and string tests. Parentheses can group expressions
when needed; use `(( ... ))` for numeric comparisons.

## `[ ... ]` versus `[[ ... ]]`

`[ ... ]` is the traditional test command (also written `test`) and is
available in POSIX shells. The closing `]` is an argument to that command, so
spaces around it and the test operators are required. Variable expansions
inside `[ ... ]` should be quoted to prevent word splitting and filename
expansion.

`[[ ... ]]` is a Bash conditional expression, not a POSIX feature. In Bash it
does not split variable expansions into separate words or expand them as
filename patterns, and it supports combining tests with `&&` and `||` inside
the expression. It also supports pattern matching on the right-hand side of
`==`; leave that pattern unquoted when you want wildcard matching. For Bash
scripts, `[[ ... ]]` is usually the clearer and safer choice. Use `[ ... ]`
when writing a script that must run under POSIX shells such as `sh`.

```{bash}
value="sample 01"

# Portable test command: quote the variable.
if [ "$value" = "sample 01" ]; then
    printf 'Exact match using [ ... ]\n'
fi

# Bash conditional: patterns on the right-hand side can match.
if [[ "$value" == sample* ]]; then
    printf 'Pattern match using [[ ... ]]\n'
fi
```

For portable shell, use separate tests joined with shell-level `&&` or `||`, or
use explicit `if`/`elif` branches.

```{bash}
input="bash/samples.tsv"

if [[ -f "$input" && -r "$input" && -s "$input" ]]; then
    printf 'Input exists, is readable, and is nonempty: %s\n' "$input"
elif [[ ! -e "$input" ]]; then
    printf 'Input does not exist: %s\n' "$input" >&2
else
    printf 'Input is not a readable, nonempty regular file: %s\n' "$input" >&2
fi
```

A way I commonly use this is to check for directories before making them if
needed. I put this at the top of my primary qmd file for a project to set up any
missing directories.
```{bash}
for directoryName in \
    output/figures/volcano_plots \
    output/figures/heatmaps \
    input/10x_flex
do
  if [[ ! -d "$directoryName" ]]; then
      mkdir -p "$directoryName"
  fi
done
```

These tests can be used directly in a loop to skip missing inputs.
```{bash}
samples=("sample_A" "sample_B")
count=0

for sample in "${samples[@]}"; do
    input="fastq/${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"
    if [[ -f "$input" ]]; then
        printf 'Found input for %s\n' "$sample"
        ((count += 1))
    else
        printf 'Missing input for %s\n' "$sample" >&2
    fi
done

if ((count > 0)); then
    printf 'Found %s input file(s)\n' "$count"
fi
```

## `while` loops and counters

A `while` loop repeats as long as its test succeeds. It is often used for
reading input line by line or for repeating a task until a condition changes.
This simple counter shows the loop structure; use a scheduler rather than a
busy loop for long-running compute tasks on a cluster.

```{bash}
count=1

while ((count <= 3)); do
    printf 'Iteration %s\n' "$count"
    ((count += 1))
done
```

# Finding files with `find`

`find` searches a directory tree and can filter paths by properties such as
name, type, or modification time. The starting directory comes first, followed
by tests. Quote filename patterns so that `find`, rather than the shell,
receives and matches the pattern.

```{bash}
find bash -type f -name '*.tsv'
find fastq -type f -name '*R1*.fastq.gz'
```

By default, `find` searches below the starting directory recursively. Add
`-maxdepth` to limit how far it descends. It can also perform an action on
matches: `-exec ... {} +` safely passes groups of matched paths to a command,
without splitting file names at spaces.

```{bash}
find bash -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.tsv' -exec wc -l {} +
```

For unusual file names, use NUL-delimited output (`-print0`) when connecting
`find` to another tool. Newlines or spaces can occur in file names, so avoid
parsing the ordinary line-oriented output of `find` into a shell word list.

# Passing file lists with `xargs`

`xargs` reads items from standard input and appends them as arguments to a
command. It is often paired with `find` to apply a command to discovered
files. Use `find -print0` with `xargs -0` so that spaces, quotes, and newlines
in file names are handled safely. The following counts lines in each TSV file
in the `bash/` folder.

```{bash}
find bash -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.tsv' -print0 |
    xargs -0 -r wc -l
```

GNU `xargs -r` avoids running the command if there are no input paths. Use
`-n 1` to pass one path per command invocation; `-P 2` can run up to two
invocations concurrently. Parallel execution is only appropriate when the
commands are independent and the available resources allow it. For many tasks,
`find -exec ... {} +` is simpler and avoids the need for `xargs`.

```{bash}
find bash -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.tsv' -print0 |
    xargs -0 -r -n 1 -P 2 wc -l
```

# Functions and arguments

Functions group reusable steps under a name. Inside a function, `$1`, `$2`,
and so on refer to the first, second, and subsequent arguments. `"$@"` is an
array thatexpands to all arguments while keeping each argument separate. Use
`local` for variables that should not leak into the rest of the script.

```{bash}
report_file() {
    local file="$1"

    if [[ -z "$file" ]]; then
        printf 'Usage: report_file FILE\n' >&2
        return 2
    fi

    printf 'File name: %s\n' "${file##*/}"
    printf 'Directory: %s\n' "$(dirname -- "$file")"
}

report_file "results/sample 01.counts.txt"
```

A function's `return` value is an exit status from 0 to 255, not a general
place to return text or large numbers. To report text, print it and capture it
with command substitution; to return success or failure, use `return`.
`"$@"` is an array of all arguments and is particularly useful for writing
wrapper functions that pass along their own arguments.

```{bash}
log_command() {
    printf 'Running:'
    printf ' %q' "$@"
    printf '\n'

    "$@"
}

# Example invocation:
log_command printf '%s\n' "This command has several arguments"
```

You may need to export the function if you want to use it in parallel or in a subshell.
```{bash}
export -f log_command
```


# Temporary files and cleanup with `mktemp` and `trap`

Temporary files are useful for intermediate results that should not be kept
with the final outputs. `mktemp -d` creates a uniquely named temporary
directory and prints its path. Saving that path in a variable lets the script
use the directory without guessing a name or accidentally reusing another
process's temporary files.

`trap` tells the shell to run a command when an event occurs. Common trap
conditions include:

| Condition          | Trigger |
| ------------------ | ---- |
| `EXIT`             | The shell is exiting, whether normally or after a handler calls `exit`. Often used for cleanup. |
| `INT`              | The process receives an interrupt signal, usually when the user presses Ctrl-C. |
| `TERM`             | The process receives a termination request, commonly from a scheduler or a `kill` command. |
| `HUP`              | The process receives a hangup signal, often when its terminal or connection closes. |
| `ERR`              | A command fails in many contexts; exact behavior depends on shell options and context. Not a substitute for checking statuses explicitly. |
| `KILL` (`SIGKILL`) | Cannot be caught or handled, so a trap cannot run when the process is forcibly killed this way. |

In this example, Ctrl-C and `TERM` cause the script to exit with conventional
status codes; the `EXIT` handler then removes the temporary directory. Keep
the path in the variable set by `mktemp`; do not point cleanup at a broad or
user-supplied directory.

```{bash}
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
trap 'rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"' EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT
trap 'exit 143' TERM

printf 'Intermediate results go in: %s\n' "$tmpdir"
```

Files created inside `"$tmpdir"` are removed by the trap as well. If you need
to inspect intermediate data after a run, copy it to a permanent output
location before the script exits. `mktemp` options vary across operating
systems; these examples target Linux systems.

# A first look at `awk`

`awk` is useful for inspecting and transforming line-oriented text, especially
tabular files. It reads input one line at a time, splits each line into fields,
and lets you print selected fields or rows that match a condition. By default,
fields are separated by whitespace: `$1` is the first field, `$2` the second,
and `$0` the entire line. Use `-F` to set a different input field separator,
such as a tab for a TSV file.

This example uses the companion `counts.tsv` file and prints the first and
third columns for rows where the third column
is at least 10. `NR` is the current line number across all input; `NR == 1`
selects the header. Setting `OFS` makes the output columns tab-delimited too.
Adjust the column numbers and condition to match your file.

```{bash}
awk -F '\t' '
    BEGIN { OFS = "\t" }
    NR == 1 { print $1, $3; next }
    $3 >= 10 { print $1, $3 }
' bash/counts.tsv
```

An `awk` program has the general form `condition { action }`. If the condition
is omitted, the action is run for every line; if the action is omitted, a
matching line is printed. The companion `samples.tsv` file in this folder
contains tab-separated sample names, conditions, and statuses. Here, `-F '\t'`
treats tabs as separators, and `$NF` refers to the last field on the current
line. These commands assume you run them from the repository root.

```{bash}
awk -F '\t' 'NR == 1 { print; next } $NF == "passed" { print }' bash/samples.tsv
```

CSV files can contain quoted fields with embedded commas, which simple field
splitting does not parse correctly. For complex CSV files, use a CSV-aware tool
or programming language rather than assuming commas always separate fields.

# A first look at `sed`

`sed` is a stream editor: it reads text and applies small editing instructions
to each line. A common use is substitution, written
`s/pattern/replacement/`. By default, the first match on each line is changed;
adding `g` changes every match on that line. These commands print transformed
text to standard output and leave the input file unchanged.

```{bash}
sed 's/old-name/new-name/g' bash/samples.tsv
sed -n '1,5p' bash/samples.tsv
```

In the second command, `-n` disables automatic printing and `1,5p` explicitly
prints lines 1 through 5. This is helpful for previewing a file or a change.
Use a different delimiter when the text contains many slashes; for example,
`|` can make paths easier to read.

```{bash}
sed 's|old-name|new-name|g' bash/samples.tsv
```

To save transformed output, write it to a different file and inspect the
result before replacing the original. Do not redirect output back to the same
file being read: the shell truncates that file before `sed` can process it.

```{bash}
sed 's/old-name/new-name/g' bash/samples.tsv > bash/samples.updated.tsv
diff -u bash/samples.tsv bash/samples.updated.tsv
```

In-place editing changes the file itself and can be harder to undo. GNU `sed`
supports making a backup with `-i.bak`; check your operating system's `sed`
documentation because the in-place option differs between GNU and BSD/macOS
versions. Make a copy or use the separate-output approach above when learning.

```{bash}
# GNU sed: edits the generated output and keeps a backup beside it
sed -i.bak 's/new-name/final-name/g' bash/samples.updated.tsv
```

# Running work in parallel

GNU `parallel` runs multiple jobs concurrently. It is useful when many
independent files need the same command. Install/use it according to your
system's guidance; clusters often provide it as a software module. Confirm
available CPUs and the cluster's policies before choosing the job count.

`pigz` is a parallel implementation of gzip. One way to use GNU `parallel` is
to run one single-threaded `pigz` process per input file, with GNU `parallel`
limiting the number of concurrent processes. Here `-k` keeps each original
uncompressed file; without it, `pigz` normally replaces the input with its
compressed version. Try this on disposable copies first.

```{bash}
find fastq -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.fastq' -print0 |
    parallel --null --jobs 4 pigz -p 1 -k
```

The `--jobs 4` setting allows up to four files to be compressed at once, while
`pigz -p 1` uses one compression thread for each file. This avoids accidentally
asking for four jobs with many threads each. If the input files already end in
`.gz`, they are already gzip-compressed and should not be passed to this
compression command.

Always consider how many CPU cores and how much memory the job uses in total.
On a shared HPC system, submit substantial work through the scheduler and
request the resources your command will use rather than launching an
unrestricted set of processes on a login node.

# Keeping terminal work alive: `screen` and `tmux`

`screen` and `tmux` are terminal multiplexers: they keep a terminal session
available when you disconnect from SSH and let you reconnect later. They are
useful for interactive work, but they are not substitutes for Slurm when
running scheduled analysis. This is a minimal `screen` workflow:

```{bash}
screen -S my-session        # start a named session
screen -ls                  # list sessions
screen -r my-session        # reconnect
screen -r                   # reconnect to the session if only one exists
```

To detach from a running `screen` session without stopping its programs, press
`Ctrl-a`, then `d`. On a shared system, reconnect only to your own session and
remember that a disconnected interactive process may still consume resources.

`tmux` provides similar functionality with different key bindings and
configuration. It is widely used, but this lesson does not assume familiarity
with it. If you choose to use it, start with its local help or a short
introductory guide and practice in a disposable session before relying on it
for important work.

# File permissions with `chmod`

Permissions control who can read, write, or execute a file. The symbolic
notation below adds execute permission for the file owner; this is commonly
needed before running a script as `./script.sh`. You can also run a script as
`bash script.sh` without changing its executable bit.

```{bash}
chmod u+x script.sh
./script.sh
```

The numeric notation uses three digits for owner, group, and others. In each
digit, read is `4`, write is `2`, and execute is `1`; add the values to combine
permissions. For example, `750` means owner can read/write/execute, group can
read/execute, and others have no access. Check the existing mode with `ls -l`
before changing it. Avoid `chmod 777`: it gives everyone write permission.

```{bash}
chmod 750 script.sh
ls -l script.sh
```

Permission changes can affect collaborators and shared data. In particular,
do not recursively change permissions on a project or data directory unless
you understand the consequences and have authorization.

# Brief introduction to Slurm array jobs

Slurm is a workload manager used by many HPC clusters. An array job submits
many similar tasks, each identified by a task ID, instead of starting a large
batch of processes on a login node. The following is a template, not a
ready-to-submit job: adapt partition, account, resources, paths, and site
requirements to your cluster.

```{bash}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=align
#SBATCH --array=0-2
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/align_%A_%a.out

samples=("sample_A" "sample_B" "sample_C")
sample="${samples[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}"

printf 'Task %s is processing %s\n' "$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID" "$sample"
# Run the real analysis command here, using the requested resources.
```

The array range above is `0-2`, so the example uses zero-based indices. Create
the `logs/` directory before submission if the cluster expects the output
directory to exist. Consult your cluster's documentation for submission, limits,
and best practices.

# Monitoring resource use

`top` displays changing process and system resource information. Press `q` to
quit. `htop` is a more visual alternative if it is installed. These tools help
you see whether a process is using CPU or memory; they do not replace scheduler
accounting or guarantee that a process is healthy.

```{bash}
top
htop
```

To check which process is yours, look at the user and command columns. On an
HPC cluster, monitor work from the appropriate compute node and use the
cluster's scheduler commands for queued and completed job status.

# Finding large directories with `du`

`du` estimates disk usage. From a directory, `du -h --max-depth=1` reports
human-readable sizes for that directory and its immediate subdirectories.
Sorting the results can make the largest entries easier to spot. Disk usage
can take time to calculate on large network filesystems, so avoid running
repeated broad scans on shared storage.

```{bash}
du -h --max-depth=1 .
du -h --max-depth=1 . | sort -h
```

The final `.` means “start here.” Replace it with a project directory you have
permission to inspect. The command reports disk usage, not necessarily the
apparent size of files; hard links, sparse files, and filesystem behavior can
make those numbers differ.

# Creating and inspecting archives with `tar`

`tar` bundles files and directories into an archive. The `-c` flag creates an
archive, `-f` names the archive, and `-v` prints files as they are added. Use
paths relative to the project directory when you want the archive to unpack
without an absolute directory structure.

```{bash}
tar cvf project-files.tar results/ scripts/ README.md
```

Add gzip compression with `-z` to create a `.tar.gz` archive. FASTQ, BAM, and
other formats that are already compressed may not shrink much further. Check
what an archive contains with `-t` before extracting it.

```{bash}
tar czvf project-files.tar.gz results/ scripts/ README.md
tar tzf project-files.tar.gz
```

Extract an archive with `-x`. By default, extraction writes into the current
directory, so first inspect the contents and choose an appropriate destination.
Only extract archives from sources you trust; archives can contain paths that
overwrite files if handled carelessly.

```{bash}
mkdir -p restored-project
tar xzf project-files.tar.gz -C restored-project
```

# Checking file checksums with `md5sum`

A checksum is a short value calculated from a file's contents. `md5sum` is
commonly used to check whether a file was transferred or copied without
accidental changes. Create a checksum file alongside a data file, then use
`--check` later to compare the current contents with the recorded checksum.

```{bash}
md5sum bash/samples.tsv > samples.tsv.md5
md5sum --check samples.tsv.md5
```

Run the check from the same directory used when creating the checksum file, or
store a path in the checksum file that will be valid from the checking
directory. MD5 is suitable for detecting accidental corruption in many
workflows, but it is not collision-resistant enough for security-sensitive
verification; use a modern hash such as SHA-256 when authenticity or
adversarial tampering matters.

# Good habits for reliable scripts

- Quote variable expansions unless you specifically need word splitting or
  wildcard expansion.
- Use arrays for lists of values, and expand them as `"${array[@]}"`.
- Test scripts with a small, disposable set of inputs before using real data.
- Make paths and resource settings explicit, especially in scheduled jobs.
- Check exit statuses and read tool output; a script finishing does not by
  itself mean that the analysis produced correct results.
